newsitem.title: ECUADOR: U.S. cargo jet crashes in Ecuador, killing 23.
newsitem.headline: U.S. cargo jet crashes in Ecuador, killing 23.

text.p: Twenty-three people were killed and 60 injured when a U.S.-owned cargo jet burst into flames and crashed into a densely populated poor district of the Ecuadorean port of Manta, officials said on Wednesday.
The Boeing 707 crew -- three Americans and a Colombian -- died, but most of the victims were on the ground.

The Pacific city 290 miles (480 km) southeast of Quito was on the eve of a fiesta when the plane caught fire soon after take-off and showered burning wreckage on the poor Dolorosa neighbourhood at 10:40 p.m. local time on Tuesday (0340 GMT on Wednesday).

The plane's wings and fuselage tore tin roofs off houses and smashed others to rubble in the crash. Rescue workers had to wait for daybreak before searching for bodies because the plane ripped out electricity lines when it crashed.
"Official figures give 23 dead after one of the injured died," Red Cross chief Javier Reyes told Reuters.

Flaming wreckage rained on eight blocks of Dolorosa -- a tragically apt name, which means "painful" in Spanish. The parish church took the brunt of the crash and shielded some of the humble houses around it from even worse damage.

"The tragedy would have been much worse if the church had not taken the impact. It would have hit houses made of bricks and wood," said one resident. "One wing hit a building by the church and as the wings are where the fuel is kept it exploded in a sheet of flames."
"All of Manta was wrapped in flames because of the fuel," another witness, Miguel Narea Zea, told Reuters.
"Part of the wing ended up just near where we live," said another. "It dragged all the houses down until it smashed into a restaurant. The owner was there and was killed."
Overstretched hospitals appealed for blood and medicine and the city morgue housed a pile of charred corpses in body bags awaiting identification.
President Abdala Bucaram declared a day of mourning and flew to Manta to supervise the rescue operations.
"This is a very regrettable accident, obviously Ecuadoran families have suffered the loss of their loved ones," he said.
Police patrolled Dolorosa to stop looting after 10 people were arrested for stealing from homes whose owners had fled.

The Boeing Co said engine makers Pratt & Whitney and the U.S. National Transportation Safety Board would travel to Manta to help determine why the plane, delivered to American Airlines in 1967 and later converted to cargo use, went down.
Boeing spokesman Dick Schleh said the 65,000 hours' flying time the plane had on the clock was "not particularly high."
The plane belonged to Millon Air, a Miami-based cargo carrier owned by a Colombian family that had no immediate comment on the crash.

Millon Air operates cargo flights, mostly by charter, to Latin American destinations. In April last year a Millon Air DC-8 overran a runway in Guatemala City and crashed into a shantytown, killing at least six people on the ground.
